new_statements.quote: 2.12. Acento. El acento en las sílabas tiene la facultad de cambiar el significado en las palabras. En el idioma Tujaal el acento es generalmente agudo y recae en la última sílaba de la palabra. Según (OKMA, 2007 :65) “El acento en el idioma Sakapulteko es fijo y cae en la última sílaba, por lo que no requiere ser representado ortográficamente (con tilde) por ser predecible”. Norma: se marca la acentuación en la última sílaba en las diferentes clases de palabras. [...] wa’-LEK / parado; xaj-WEK / bailó; qa-JEK / bajó; mal-Q’AB’ / anillo [...] En las palabras que están seguidas por partículas o clíticos y que están ligados fonológicamente, el acento cae en estas palabras. [...] xajk’iyUUL / crecimos; kinb’antajUUL / vengo de regreso; kirya’AN / lo da
new_statements.translation: 2.12. Accent. Accent on syllables has the capacity to change the meaning of words. In the Tujaal language the accent is generally oxytone and falls on the last syllable of the word. According to OKMA (2007:65): 'Stress in the Sakapulteko language is fixed and falls on the last syllable, so it does not need to be represented orthographically (with an accent mark) because it is predictable.' Rule: stress is placed on the last syllable in the various word classes. [...] wa'-LEK 'standing'; xaj-WEK 'danced'; qa-JEK 'went down'; mal-Q'AB' 'ring' [...] In words followed by particles or clitics that are phonologically bound, the stress falls on these [particles/clitics]. [...] xajk'iyUUL 'we grew'; kinb'antajUUL 'I come back'; kirya'AN 'gives it (upward)'
new_statements.citation: López López, Ana Estefany / Comunidad Lingüística Sakapulteka-Tujaal, Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala (ALMG). 2023. Rikemiik Ritz'ib'siik li Tziij Tujaal. Actualización de la Gramática Normativa Sakapulteko/Tujaal. Sacapulas: ALMG, Dirección de Lingüística y Comunicación. 212 pp. (quoting Mó Isém / OKMA 2007. Rikemiik li Tujaal Tziij: Gramática Sakapulteka, p. 65)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (212 pp., Word-generated text layer; PDF page n = printed page n). extracted text of p. 59 gives, verbatim: "2.12. Acento / El acento en las sílabas tiene la facultad de cambiar el significado en las palabras. En el idioma Tujaal el acento es generalmente agudo y recae en la última sílaba de la palabra. Según (OKMA, 2007 :65) “El acento en el idioma Sakapulteko es fijo y cae en la última sílaba, por lo que no requiere ser representado ortográficamente (con tilde) por ser predecible”. / Norma: se marca la acentuación en la última sílaba en las diferentes clases de palabras." followed by the examples wa’-lek / parado, xaj-wek / bailó, qa-jek / bajó, mal-q’ab’ / anillo, much’-b’aam / ta…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word; when a phonologically bound particle or enclitic follows, stress moves to that final element (the stress domain is the phonological word including enclitics). Stress is predictable and not marked in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the ALMG 2023 grammar. Bennett 2016:497 (survey) notes that Sakapultek is one of the few Mayan languages where secondary stress may have word-level phonological consequences, citing DuBois 1981:99,124,144-55 (not seen first-hand).
new_statements.exceptions: The opening sentence says syllable accent 'can change the meaning of words', but the chapter introduction (ch. II) states the accent is not written because no words whose meaning depends on accent have been found; the text says 'generalmente' (generally) final without listing exceptions. Bennett 2016 notes loanword/non-final exceptions for K'ichean generally (Kaqchikel), not specifically for Sakapultek.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms), with explicit extension to the word + bound particle/clitic string; nothing on phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2023 ALMG normative grammar uses the community's own name "Tujaal" for the language; it is the same language as Sakapulteko/Sacapultec (saca1238), spoken in Sacapulas, Quiché. The quoted OKMA 2007 passage refers to it as "Sakapulteko".

sources.note: §2.12 Acento, p. 59: stress is generally acute/final, on the last syllable of the word; quotes OKMA 2007:65 that stress is fixed on the final syllable, predictable, not written; with phonologically bound particles/clitics the stress falls on the clitic (xajk'iyUUL, kinb'antajUUL, kirya'AN). Ch. II intro (p. 17-18 area) says accent is not written because no minimal pairs by stress were found.

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2016. Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10): 469-514. doi:10.1111/lnc3.12148
sources.note: p. 476: 'Unstressed long vowels are freely allowed in Sakapultek (final stress)' (data from DuBois 1981, Mó Isém 2007); p. 495: final stress is the norm in K'ichean; p. 497: Sakapultek is one of a handful of Mayan languages where secondary stress may have word-level phonological consequences (DuBois 1981:99,124,144-55). Survey, second-hand.
Consonant/vowel inventory only; nothing on stress; cites DuBois 1981 and Mó Isém 2006.
